title: China Deploys $9 Billion in State Funds to Prop Up Markets After AI-Driven Selloff
excerpt: Two state investment firms pledged to continue buying as the Shanghai Composite rebounds from a 5.8% weekly drop, with the tech-heavy ChiNext index down 21% this month.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • China deployed nearly $9 billion to stabilize markets after a significant selloff in tech stocks.
  • The Shanghai Composite dropped 7.3% in July, while the ChiNext index fell 21% this month.
  • State-backed firms remain optimistic and will continue buying shares in key sectors.
  • Government intervention led to a 0.85% rebound in the Shanghai Composite on Monday.
  • Analysts caution that state buying cannot resolve deeper structural economic issues.

  • China Reform Holdings and China Chengtong Holdings deployed nearly $9 billion combined — $7.38 billion and $1.48 billion respectively — to buy Chinese equities and stabilise markets.
  • The move came after a brutal selloff that saw the Shanghai Composite shed 7.3% in July and the tech-heavy ChiNext index plunge 21%, driven by global fears over AI spending sustainability.
  • Both state-backed firms, part of China's "national team" of market stabilisers, pledged to continue increasing stakes in state-owned enterprises and technology stocks.
  • The Shanghai Composite rebounded 0.85% on Monday following the intervention, though analysts warn that government buying alone cannot resolve deeper structural issues.

State Investors Step In

China's government deployed its familiar playbook for stabilising tumbling stock markets over the weekend, with two major state-owned capital operators announcing nearly $9 billion in fresh equity purchases.

China Reform Holdings Corp said Sunday that entities under its investment arm have tapped more than 50 billion yuan ($7.38 billion) from special relending facilities and matching funds for share buybacks and stake increases. Separately, China Chengtong Holdings Group announced purchases of nearly 10 billion yuan ($1.48 billion) in Chinese stocks.

Both firms declared they remain "firmly optimistic" about the prospects of China's capital markets and will continue buying shares in centrally administered state-owned enterprises and technology companies — a clear signal that Beijing's tolerance for further declines has been reached.

The trigger was not unique to China."**

"The STAR Market, home to many of China's leading chipmakers, has plunged roughly 25% from its July 1 peak, wiping out over 4 trillion yuan in market value.</p> <p>The trigger was not unique to China."

What Triggered the Rout

The intervention followed a punishing stretch for Chinese equities, driven by a global selloff in AI and technology stocks as investors grew increasingly unsettled about the sustainability of massive artificial-intelligence infrastructure spending.

The benchmark Shanghai Composite Index dropped 5.8% last week alone and has shed 7.3% so far in July. The pain was far worse in the technology sector: the ChiNext Price Index, China's equivalent of the Nasdaq, has slumped 21% this month. The STAR Market, home to many of China's leading chipmakers, has plunged roughly 25% from its July 1 peak, wiping out over 4 trillion yuan in market value.

The trigger was not unique to China. Across global markets, investors have begun questioning whether the enormous capital expenditure on AI infrastructure — from data centres to advanced chips — will generate returns proportional to the investment. That reassessment hit Chinese tech stocks particularly hard, given the sector's heavy reliance on government support and its more fragile investor base.

The 'National Team' Playbook

China's "national team" — a loosely defined network of state-linked investment entities led by institutions like Central Huijin Investment — has a well-established track record of intervening during market stress. The group first formed in response to a dramatic market crash in 2015 and has been mobilised repeatedly since.

Impact of State Intervention
›Shanghai Composite rebounded 0.85% after intervention.
›ChiNext index rose 0.4% following state buying.
›State-backed firms optimistic about market prospects.
›Intervention aims to establish a market floor.

Analysts say Monday's coordinated announcements were designed to establish a market floor and signal policymakers' determination to maintain capital market stability. The Shanghai Composite ended Monday 0.85% higher, while the ChiNext rose 0.4%, suggesting the intervention had at least a short-term calming effect.

"CRHC remains firmly confident in the outlook for China's capital markets and will continue to use the relending programme, alongside its own funds, to increase holdings."

— China Reform Holdings Corp statement

Implications for Global and Indian Markets

For investors in India and across Asia, China's market turmoil and the government's response carry broader implications. A sustained Chinese selloff could drag Asian markets lower through contagion effects, while a successful stabilisation might restore some calm to the region's equity markets.

Market Trends and Concerns
›Global selloff in AI stocks triggered market downturn.
›Investors question sustainability of AI infrastructure spending.
›China's tech sector heavily reliant on government support.
›Historical interventions buy time but don't fix underlying issues.

Indian markets, already navigating their own Q1 earnings season alongside oil price volatility from the US-Iran conflict, have shown relative resilience. But China's experience underscores a global risk: the AI investment boom that has driven technology stocks higher across markets may be entering a period of reckoning as investors demand proof that the spending will pay off.

What's Next

Analysts warn that while state buying can establish a short-term floor, it cannot substitute for addressing deeper structural issues in China's economy, including a prolonged property downturn and weak consumer confidence. Historical precedent suggests the national team's interventions buy time but don't reverse underlying trends. In 2015, similar buying steadied markets temporarily, but it took years for blue-chip indices to recover their peaks. Investors will be watching whether Beijing follows the liquidity injection with more substantive policy measures.
